title: A card game that counts rising runs
hook: Deal eight cards into piles. The number of piles answers a question you never asked.

doesNotKnow: that a card game finds the longest rising run with skips

misconception: The longest rising sequence starts at the smallest number.
objective: The learner can explain that dealing 3 1 4 1 5 9 2 6 onto the leftmost pile whose top is not smaller makes 4 piles, that a rising run uses at most one card per pile, and that back-pointers give a run as long as the number of piles, so the longest rising run has 4 cards (e.g. 3 4 5 9 or 1 4 5 6).

claims.text: Dealing 3 1 4 1 5 9 2 6 onto the leftmost pile whose top is not smaller makes 4 piles.
claims.source: Builder's node script (scratchpad checks/all.mjs): piles [3,1,1] [4,2] [5] [9,6]. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 10): Own node deal: [3,1,1] [4,2] [5] [9,6].

claims.text: The longest rising run (each card bigger than the last, skipping allowed) in 3 1 4 1 5 9 2 6 has 4 cards, for example 1 4 5 6 or 3 4 5 9.
claims.source: Builder's node dynamic programming over the 8 cards: longest strictly increasing subsequence length 4. Both examples checked by hand against the order of the cards. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 10): Own O(n^2) DP: LIS = 4; 1 4 5 6 and 3 4 5 9 are both increasing subsequences in order (node).

claims.text: A longest rising run need not start at the smallest card.
claims.source: 3 4 5 9 has length 4, the maximum (c2), and starts with 3 while the smallest card is 1. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 10): Follows from c2: 3 4 5 9 is maximal and starts at 3, not the minimum 1.

claims.text: A rising run can use at most one card from each pile, since each pile goes downward.
claims.source: Cards on a pile are placed on tops not smaller than themselves, so each pile is non-increasing from bottom to top in deal order; two cards of a strictly rising run cannot both lie on one pile. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 10): Piles are non-increasing; a strictly increasing run cannot take two cards from one pile (equal 1s included).

claims.text: Every card on pile k points back to a smaller, earlier card on pile k - 1, so a run as long as the number of piles always exists: the number of piles equals the length of the longest rising run.
claims.source: When a card lands on pile k, the top of pile k - 1 is smaller (else the card would have gone there) and was dealt earlier. Aldous and Diaconis, 'Longest increasing subsequences: from patience sorting to the Baik-Deift-Johansson theorem', Bull. AMS 36 (1999). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 10): Back-pointer argument re-derived; own node check: piles = LIS length on 20,000 random sequences with repeats. Aldous and Diaconis, Bull. AMS 36(4) (1999). Stage trace from pile 4 gives 1 4 5 6.

recall.question: You deal a row of cards into piles, each card on the leftmost pile whose top is not smaller, and end with 6 piles. What does that tell you?
options: The longest rising run (with skips) has 6 cards
There are 6 cards smaller than the first
recall.why: A rising run takes at most one card from each pile, and the back-pointers always build a run with one card per pile, so the pile count is the longest run's length.
